books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution, Section 2 (ratified 1868)

stimulus.text:
“Representatives shall be apportioned among the several States according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each State, excluding Indians not taxed. But when the right to vote at any election for the choice of electors for President and Vice-President of the United States, Representatives in Congress, the Executive and Judicial officers of a State, or the members of the Legislature thereof, is denied to any of the male inhabitants of such State, being twenty-one years of age, and citizens of the United States, or in any way abridged, except for participation in rebellion, or other crime, the basis of representation therein shall be reduced...”

—Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2, ratified 1868
stimulus.source_note: Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2, ratified 1868. Public domain. Wording verified against the Constitution Annotated (Congress.gov). Trailing ellipsis marks omitted text.

rationales.A: Background: Stone and Blackwell supported Reconstruction and the Republican Party, not opposition to it.
rationales.B: Stone and Blackwell were disappointed by the amendment too, but they argued that a partial victory was worth taking. They believed women’s suffrage could be won state by state, while the Republican Party protected Black men’s new rights.
rationales.C: Background: they stayed with the Republican Party, which they saw as the party of Reconstruction.
rationales.D: Background: no new constitutional convention was on the table; their plan was state-by-state work.
rationales.general:
1. Stone and Blackwell shared Stanton and Anthony’s disappointment.
2. But they read the same amendment differently: a step forward is still forward.
3. Background: their plan was to take the Black vote now and win the woman’s vote state by state.
4. So the split was over tactics, not over the goal.
Remember: allies can agree on the goal and still split over whether to take half a loaf.
